caption:
Government investigators got ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok to produce attack plans in under 12 hours, a GAO report released November 18 says.
All four refused at first, then common bypass tricks worked.
The companies say the tested models have since been replaced, and Sen. Maggie Hassan plans AI safety hearings.

Should AI companies have to report users who try this?

paragraphs.text: Four of the most widely used AI chatbots produced plans for attacks in the United States during covert tests by the Government Accountability Office, according to a GAO report released on November 18, 2026. The Washington Sun reported that investigators posing as regular users got ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok to generate plans with named targets, locations and methods in less than 12 hours.

The testing took place in spring 2026 and was the watchdog's first covert test of AI platforms, according to the Washington Sun. The report was requested by Sen. Maggie Hassan, a New Hampshire Democrat who is the incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.

Each chatbot was randomly assigned one of two scenarios: a bombing meant to cause mass casualties or an attack meant to cause economic damage. All four platforms initially refused to plan a violent attack. Investigators then used what the report called common safeguard bypassing techniques, which it did not name, and paid for upgraded subscriptions on at least three of the platforms, the Washington Sun reported.
The GAO did not publish its prompts or techniques, and it did not say which chatbot produced which plan, in order to keep others from repeating the tests.

Two platforms planned vehicle bomb attacks, one on a hotel parking garage and one on a convention center in major U.S. cities. According to Kevin Walsh, a GAO director who co-signed the report, both chose a date and time and offered tips on avoiding law enforcement. The other two platforms chose electrical substations in a major U.S. city as targets, one proposing a drone strike and the other gunfire. One estimated billions of dollars in damage, and one produced a map with targets circled.

The GAO described the plans as largely viable. A bomb squad commander said both bomb recipes would result in an explosion, and investigators found the needed materials for sale at stores the chatbots suggested. The plans also contained errors, including a convention center date with no scheduled event, a map with roads in the wrong places and substations protected by high walls. The GAO said the details were not novel and much of the information is available online, but that plans which could have taken weeks or months were assembled in hours.

Anthropic said it takes the findings seriously and does not dispute that a determined tester can sometimes get harmful content from an AI system, but said it could not verify the GAO's results. It also noted that the GAO did not compare the chatbots' answers with what ordinary web searches would return. Google said the testing used earlier models. OpenAI said the report does not always make clear which parts of a plan came from ChatGPT and said it reran the reviewed requests on its newer GPT-6 Astra model, which generally gave more refusals. The maker of Grok said successful jailbreaks require adversarial prompting.

According to the Washington Sun, only one company suspended the investigators' accounts. Two removed parts of the chats within days, though the GAO could not tell whether that was deliberate. Walsh said account suspensions that come days or weeks later may come too late.

Hassan said AI safety legislation will be among the first areas of focus when she takes over the committee, and that an early hearing on AI threats to homeland security and critical infrastructure is planned for after the new Congress convenes in January. She called for rules that keep models from being released without adequate safeguards and for companies to report illegal activity to law enforcement.

The report does not show that chatbots invent new attack methods; the GAO itself says the details were not novel. What it does show is speed and packaging: four mainstream products, each tested once, turned scattered public information into organized plans within half a day after their first refusal was bypassed. That framing, rather than any single answer, is likely to shape the hearings, along with the question of whether companies should act faster when an account is clearly being used to plan harm.
The next marker is Hassan's first committee hearing on AI threats in early 2027, where companies may be pressed on account suspensions and on reporting illegal activity to law enforcement.
